title: Fox Television Stations, Inc. v. FCC
lead: After the Supreme Court upheld an agency policy change as adequately explained, broadcasters returned to the Second Circuit with constitutional objections. That court invalidated the indecency policy for vagueness, a ruling later vacated on further review.

actors.name: Fox Television Stations and other networks

proceedings: 2006 agency reconsideration maintained two Billboard findings.
2007 administrative-law reversal was reversed by Supreme Court in 2009.
2010 Second Circuit granted petition and vacated order and policy; Supreme Court later vacated in 2012 on narrower fair-notice grounds.
limits: Historical 2010 stage, not final operative broad constitutional judgment. Unanimous panel; Leval’s dissent concerned 2007. Profanity abandoned, scope of Pacifica and blanket strict scrutiny unresolved.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Restrained enforcement changes after a live awards remark
paragraphs: Federal law prohibited obscene, indecent, or profane broadcasts, with civil forfeitures available to the Federal Communications Commission. The Supreme Court’s earlier Pacifica broadcast-indecency decision sustained action against repeated George Carlin expletives in a particular afternoon broadcast, emphasizing that narrow context. The Commission initially focused on seven words, brought no enforcement actions from 1978 through 1987, and later adopted contextual review while remaining restrained toward isolated nonliteral expletives.

Its 2001 guidance considered sexual or excretory description and patent offensiveness, examining explicitness, repetition, and pandering, titillation, or shock. After Bono’s fleeting remark at the 2003 Golden Globes, the Commission’s 2004 order treated the F-word as inherently sexual even nonliterally and removed the ordinary protection for fleeting use. It also revised profanity doctrine, later abandoned for this appeal. Congress increased maximum fines from $32,500 to $325,000, and separate licensee broadcasts could accumulate violations. Those potential penalties were not a fine imposed against Fox here.

sections.title: Fox’s broadcasts pass through agency and judicial review
paragraphs: A 2006 omnibus order applied the changed approach to Fox’s 2002 and 2003 Billboard Music Awards, NYPD Blue, and The Early Show. Cher’s unscripted acceptance speech and Nicole Richie’s award presentation used expletives the agency considered explicit, shocking, and gratuitous despite brevity.

After petitions and voluntary remand, the November 6 reconsideration maintained the Billboard findings. It reversed The Early Show finding for a bona fide news interview, while rejecting an absolute news exemption, and dismissed the NYPD Blue complaint because the complainant’s Eastern-time broadcast occurred within safe-harbor hours. That was different from the later-reviewed nudity forfeiture.

The Second Circuit’s 2007 majority found inadequate administrative explanation without reaching constitutionality. The Supreme Court reversed in 2009 under the Administrative Procedure Act and remanded constitutional questions. The 2010 panel therefore examined notice, chilling, and enforcement discretion rather than repeating its rejected administrative-law conclusion. Only one of three captioned dockets remained; the others were moot.

sections.title: The court finds the factors and exceptions unpredictable
paragraphs: Judge Pooler’s unanimous panel considered changed media and parental-blocking technology but remained bound by Pacifica. It neither imposed strict scrutiny on every broadcast restriction nor decided Pacifica’s outer regulatory boundary. Broadcasting’s different treatment did not eliminate fair-notice rights, while an earlier internet-indecency decision did not automatically resolve the agency’s more developed contextual test.

The court found decisions often recited factors without explaining why one sexual or excretory expression crossed the line and another did not. Flexibility to address new expressions did not excuse standards broadcasters could not predict. The court did not require restoration of a fixed seven-word list.

Exceptions to presumptive F-word and S-word bans were similarly uncertain. Repeated language in Saving Private Ryan served realism, while musicians’ actual speech in The Blues was not deemed educationally necessary. The same morning-news interview changed from indecent to excused. Qualified agency predictions about a hypothetical teenage educational program supplied little assurance where protected speech and major penalties were at stake.

Broad discretion also risked subjective content discrimination. The panel did not find or suspect actual viewpoint suppression; it found the policy insufficiently constrained that possibility. Context and promises to defer to news judgment supplied no dependable limiting standard.

sections.title: The record shows effects beyond awards shows
sections.cue: Broad vacatur followed by a narrower Supreme Court stage
paragraphs: Stations withheld or limited a September 11 documentary, a novel reading, local debate, memorial coverage, live news, and sexuality discussions. Fox had precleared scripts and used audio delay, but Richie’s rapid unscripted remarks defeated bleeping. Absolute prevention could require abandoning live coverage or controversial speakers, with consequences for public affairs and art. These were examples of chilling, not merely a preference for offensive language.

On July 13, 2010 the panel granted review and vacated the challenged order and underlying policy as impermissibly vague under the First Amendment, leaving the Commission free to devise a constitutional policy. Judges Leval and Hall joined; Leval’s dissent belonged to the earlier 2007 decision.

The Supreme Court subsequently vacated this 2010 judgment in 2012 and supplied a narrower fair-notice ruling. The Second Circuit’s broad invalidation thus remains a distinct stage in the chronology, not the final disposition of the dispute.
